intro: The finale opens with an accented Ukrainian song. A broad violin melody repeatedly interrupts the dance, then returns in B♭ major at the close of the concerto.

sections.label: A · Piano, accented dance theme
sections.mNote: The finale opens with a Ukrainian tune in B♭ minor.

sections.label: B · Contrasting violin melody in D♭ major
sections.mNote: The violins introduce the contrasting tune in D♭ major.

sections.label: A′ · Piano’s B♭-minor dance theme returns
sections.mNote: Descending scales lead back to the clipped B♭-minor tune.

sections.label: B′ · Broad theme in E♭ major
sections.mNote: The broad tune returns a tone higher.

sections.label: A″ · Refrain, extended
sections.mNote: The refrain returns with scales, arpeggios and a longer build.

sections.label: Link · Piano octaves prepare B♭
sections.mNote: Octave runs in the piano lead to the broad final theme.

sections.label: B″ · Broad melody, full orchestra, B♭ major
sections.mNote: The broad melody returns in B♭ major.

sections.label: Coda · Allegro vivo to the end
sections.mNote: Quick piano figures and orchestral chords close in B♭ major.

cues.title: Piano entry, Ukrainian song
cues.text: After a brief orchestral opening, the piano enters with a Ukrainian song, Go on, go on Ivan. The B♭-minor dance theme is built from short phrases with displaced accents.
cues.evidence: Ukrainian song identified under Related Works at https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/index.php?title=Piano_Concerto_No._1. Opening and piano theme: https://tonic-chord.com/tchaikovsky-piano-concerto-no-1-analysis/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Second theme in D♭ major
cues.text: The violins introduce a broad second theme in D♭ major, and the piano then takes it up. Its long notes follow the short phrases of the dance theme. The melody returns in B♭ major near the end of the movement.
cues.evidence: Finale’s D♭-major second theme, violin and piano statements, and eventual B♭-major return: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Folk-song source, 1869
cues.text: In 1869 Tchaikovsky arranged the Russian folk song “I’m Coming to the Capital” for piano duet as No. 30 of his Fifty Russian Folksongs. A variant of its tune is thought to be the source of the finale’s broad violin melody.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky Research, Piano Concerto No. 1 (Related Works): the finale’s second subject “may have been derived from” the folk song arranged in 1869 as No. 30 of the Fifty Russian Folksongs. The page on the Fifty Russian Folksongs (arranged August–September 1869, piano duet) repeats it: a variant of the tune may be the finale’s second subject. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Piano_Concerto_No._1 https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Fifty_Russian_Folksongs

cues.title: Second theme in E♭ major
cues.text: The broad melody returns in E♭ major, a tone above its first appearance. Descending scales lead back to the piano’s B♭-minor dance.
cues.evidence: Finale, second appearance of the contrasting theme in E♭ major and descending transition: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky); bars 133–158 in https://tonic-chord.com/tchaikovsky-piano-concerto-no-1-analysis/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Aleksandr Ziloti, 1889
cues.text: In January 1889 Tchaikovsky told the pianist Aleksandr Ziloti that he had altered a passage in this finale, “der verfluchte Stelle”, the accursed place. “I think it will be shorter and better,” he wrote. He had composed the concerto fourteen years earlier.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky to Aleksandr Ziloti, letter 3751, 27 December 1888/8 January 1889, in the translation printed in Tchaikovsky Research, Piano Concerto No. 1 (Composition, third version): “In the finale, I have now altered der verfluchte Stelle; I think it will be shorter and better”. The recording’s performing edition is unspecified. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Piano_Concerto_No._1

cues.title: Octave passage before B♭ major
cues.text: The piano plays rapid octaves across the keyboard during the long preparation for B♭ major. The broad tune does not return until this passage ends.
cues.evidence: Finale’s extended preparation and octave passage before the B♭-major culmination: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter from Bülow, January 1876
cues.text: On 13 January 1876 Bülow replied to Tchaikovsky’s thoughts of revising the concerto that “no changes are necessary,” apart from some extra piano notes in a few tutti, which he had already added himself. His one comment on the finale concerned the tempo of the “triumphal 2nd motif” before the last stretta.
cues.evidence: Bülow to Tchaikovsky, 1/13 January 1876, in the translation printed in Tchaikovsky Research, Piano Concerto No. 1 (Composition, second version). https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Piano_Concerto_No._1

cues.title: Second theme in B♭ major
cues.text: The broad melody returns in B♭ major, played by piano and orchestra together. This violin tune first interrupted the dance, and it now carries the concerto’s closing pages.
cues.evidence: Finale’s culminating second-theme statement in B♭ major: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Coda, Allegro vivo
cues.text: The marking changes to Allegro vivo. Rapid piano figures lead into the final B♭-major chords, and the concerto closes on a dominant–tonic cadence.
cues.evidence: Final coda marking and perfect authentic cadence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Violins enter with the D♭-major melody
transitions.to: B · Contrasting violin melody in D♭ major
transitions.how: The transition passes through F major. The violins then begin their broad melody in D♭ major. The piano takes up the tune after them in long notes, which replace the short accented figures of the refrain.
transitions.evidence: Finale bars 45–79: https://tonic-chord.com/tchaikovsky-piano-concerto-no-1-analysis/. Violin and piano statements: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky).

transitions.title: Down the scales to B♭ minor
transitions.from: B · Contrasting violin melody in D♭ major
transitions.to: A′ · Piano’s B♭-minor dance theme returns
transitions.how: Descending scales lead away from the D♭-major melody. The harmony moves through F major to B♭ minor, and the piano’s dance returns in a shortened form.
transitions.evidence: Finale bars 80–101: https://tonic-chord.com/tchaikovsky-piano-concerto-no-1-analysis/; descending scales described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky).

transitions.title: The broad tune returns in E♭
transitions.from: A′ · Piano’s B♭-minor dance theme returns
transitions.to: B′ · Broad theme in E♭ major
transitions.how: After the dance’s intervening episodes, the broad melody returns in E♭ major in bars 133–149. Its longer notes again stand apart from the piano’s quick writing. The tune now sits a tone above its first statement in D♭ major.

transitions.title: The refrain returns after descending scales
transitions.from: B′ · Broad theme in E♭ major
transitions.how: Descending scales lead the music from the E♭-major theme back towards B♭ minor. The piano plays the refrain again, then a longer succession of scales and arpeggios that leads into the coda.
transitions.evidence: Finale bars 150–214: https://tonic-chord.com/tchaikovsky-piano-concerto-no-1-analysis/; descending transition described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky).

transitions.title: Approach to the octave passage
transitions.how: The refrain’s cadence opens a long preparation for B♭ major. Scales and arpeggios in the piano lead into rapid octaves, and the broad tune’s final return is held back while the orchestra builds up behind the soloist.
transitions.evidence: Finale’s extended transition and octave writing before the B♭-major culmination: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky).

transitions.title: Dominant preparation to the B♭-major melody
transitions.to: B″ · Broad melody, full orchestra, B♭ major
transitions.how: The long dominant preparation resolves into the broad melody in B♭ major. Piano and orchestra share the statement. The tune, first played quietly by the violins, is now taken up by the whole ensemble.
transitions.evidence: Dominant prolongation and final B♭-major second-theme statement: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky).

transitions.title: Allegro vivo and final cadence
transitions.from: B″ · Broad melody, full orchestra, B♭ major
transitions.to: Coda · Allegro vivo to the end
transitions.how: The broad melody gives way to the Allegro vivo. The piano plays quick figures against emphatic orchestral chords, and the last bars close in B♭ major with a perfect cadence from F to B♭.
transitions.evidence: Finale’s concluding Allegro vivo and perfect authentic cadence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky).

composer.epithet: Composer who could write a brilliant ballroom scene and, within it, a single melody showing that someone present was unhappy.
facts: School of Jurisprudence; Saint Petersburg Conservatory, 1862–65, with Anton Rubinstein and Nikolai Zaremba
Nadezhda von Meck: an allowance, 1877–90, and a friendship conducted by letter
Three ballets; Eugene Onegin, The Queen of Spades and other operas
composer.background:
At Kamenka on 6 July 1878, Tchaikovsky was explaining to Nadezhda von Meck how he composed. Ideas came to him in the middle of conversations, and he kept them in his head until he could sketch them on the first sheet of paper to hand. He held that waiting for the right mood was no way to work. “Inspiration is a guest who does not like to visit the idle,” he told her. He then stopped for dinner. At two o’clock he resumed, and went on to sketching, orchestration, fair copies and how far a symphony must keep to its traditional form.

He was born in Votkinsk, where his father managed an ironworks. He grew deeply attached to his French governess, Fanny Dürbach, and began piano lessons at the end of 1845. The profession chosen for him was the law. In 1850 he entered the preparatory class of the Imperial School of Jurisprudence in Saint Petersburg. Four years later his mother died of cholera. He graduated in 1859 and took a post at the Ministry of Justice, while giving more and more of his time to opera and concerts.
